subject: Career
title: Death by Meeting: Why Most Meetings Fail
description: A tiny lesson with a big payoff: Death by Meeting: Why Most Meetings Fail.

hook.text: Executives spend 23 hours per week in meetings. A Harvard study found 71% of those are unproductive.

buildup.text: Most meetings fail for the same reasons: no agenda, wrong people, no decisions, and no follow-up.

discovery.text: Jeff Bezos's two-pizza rule: if two pizzas can't feed the group, the meeting has too many people.

twist.text: The silent cost: a one-hour meeting with ten people costs ten person-hours. Multiply by yearly meetings.

climax.text: Every meeting needs: a purpose statement, an agenda, the minimum attendees, and a documented outcome.

punchline.text: If a meeting has no agenda, it has no purpose.

quiz.question: What percentage of meetings are unproductive according to Harvard research?

details.summary: Patrick Lencioni's 'Death by Meeting' framework argues that meetings fail because organizations blend decision-making, brainstorming, and status updates into single unfocused sessions. Separating meeting types into distinct formats dramatically improves their effectiveness.
details.whyItMatters: The average worker spends over fifteen hours per week in meetings, and seventy percent report that most are unproductive. Structured meeting types reclaim enormous amounts of lost time.
takeaways: Separate tactical check-ins from strategic discussions
Daily standups should last no more than fifteen minutes
Quarterly off-sites are ideal for long-range strategic planning

faq.question: What are the four meeting types Lencioni recommends?
faq.answer: Lencioni proposes the daily check-in for five minutes, the weekly tactical for up to sixty minutes, the monthly strategic for two hours of deep debate, and the quarterly off-site review for big-picture assessment. Each has a distinct purpose and format.

faq.question: How do I convince my team to adopt a structured meeting approach?
faq.answer: Start with a two-week pilot. Track total meeting hours, decisions made, and perceived productivity before and after. Quantifiable improvement in decision speed and reduced meeting hours typically builds enough support for permanent adoption.
